newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia Sugar-Traders watch for buyers of Brazil sugar.
newsitem.headline: Asia Sugar-Traders watch for buyers of Brazil sugar.

text.p: Asia's sugar markets were quiet as traders' attention turned to possible large purchases of Brazilian sugar, regional sources said on Wednesday.
The Pakistani government was more likely to purchase from Brazil than China, because China's prices were seen as less competitive, traders said.
"I don't think the government is willing to pay the premium (for Chinese sugar)," a trader said, adding that Brazil would be a more serious contender.
On Monday, the state-run Trading Corporation of Pakistan invited bids, to be opened on May 24, for 50,000 tonnes of white refined crystal sugar.
Traders earlier said China had sold three to four cargoes of 13,000 to 14,000 tonnes each of white sugar to Pakistan at a high premium.
Chinese white sugar to Pakistan was heard offered at US$375 per tonne, C&F Karachi, while Thai sugar was pegged at $360 to $365 per tonne, C&F Karachi. No firm Brazilian offers were heard.
Tokyo sugar traders said they would remain sidelined until uncertainty cleared over whether U.S. trade house Cargill would find buyers for Brazilian and Central American raw sugar.
"People in the market think the destinations (of Brazilian sugar) are mostly to the Black Sea," said a senior sugar trader in China.

On Tuesday, talk that Cargill would find buyers for more than 300,000 tonnes of Brazilian and Central American raw sugar may have underpinned positive sentiment in the New York sugar market, traders said.

"We'll hesitate to trade until the clear picture about Cargill deals (is) available. Thai premiums are weaker this week as local players are sidelined," a sugar trader at a major Japan trade house said.
Thai raw sugar premiums for May/July delivery were quoted at 0.55/0.60 cents per pound (bid/offer) over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange (CSCE) May futures on a free-on-board (FOB) basis.
In comparison, last week's Thai raw sugar premiums for May/July delivery were quoted at 0.65/0.75 cents per pound (bid/offer) over New York's CSCE on a FOB basis.
July/September deliveries this week were quoted at 0.45/0.55 cents, down from last week's 0.57/0.65 cents.
Premiums had softened with little regional demand and shifts in players' positions.

"People who were long sugar were hoping to squeeze out the raws and were hoping for buying, but the problem is there were no nominations to buy and now (the longs) are panicking," one Hong Kong trader said.
Most of the sugar heading to China from Thailand was intended for tolling, with one ship currently heard loading 14,000 tonnes of raw sugar in Thailand.

A senior trader in China said the Chinese government was still considering buying another 400,000 tonnes of sugar for national stocks in a bid to boost domestic sugar prices, but others dismissed the move as "pure talk".
The China trader noted that regular government reserve replacements of old sugar with new could also affect prices.
"In warehouses every year, (the government) will sell old sugar (at lower prices) and buy new sugar, that is a factor affecting the sugar price," he said.
The U.S. Agriculture Department on Tuesday estimated 1997/98 world centrifugal sugar production at 122.4 million tonnes (raw value), up slightly from a revised 122.3 million tonnes seen for 1996/97.
"Unlike grains, USDA's sugar output estimates are unlikely to affect the market so much," another trader said.
--Mishi Saran in Hong Kong (852) 2843 6358
--Eiichiro Tokumoto in Tokyo (813) 3432 7391
